title: Getting Started with Computer Networking
excerpt: An introduction to networking fundamentals — from LAN setup to understanding the OSI model and TCP/IP protocols.
content:
Computer networking is the backbone of modern IT infrastructure. Whether you're setting up a small home network or configuring enterprise-grade systems, understanding the fundamentals is essential.

What is a Computer Network?

A computer network is a collection of interconnected devices that share resources and communicate with each other using defined protocols. Networks can range from a simple two-device connection to complex global systems spanning thousands of nodes.

The OSI Model

The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model is a conceptual framework that standardizes network communication into seven layers:

  • Physical Layer — Cables, switches, and raw bit transmission
  • Data Link Layer — MAC addressing, frames, error detection
  • Network Layer — IP addressing, routing (IP, ICMP)
  • Transport Layer — TCP/UDP, port numbers, reliability
  • Session Layer — Session management
  • Presentation Layer — Data formatting, encryption
  • Application Layer — HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS

TCP/IP Protocol

TCP/IP is the practical model used in real-world networks. It condenses the OSI layers into four: Link, Internet, Transport, and Application. Understanding TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) is fundamental to network troubleshooting.

Practical Tips

Here are some essential commands for network troubleshooting:

ping 8.8.8.8        # Test connectivity
ipconfig /all       # View network config
nslookup google.com # DNS lookup
tracert google.com  # Trace route

Mastering these fundamentals will give you a strong foundation for any IT career. In future posts, we'll dive deeper into VLAN configuration, MikroTik router setup, and advanced troubleshooting techniques.

title: Troubleshooting Common PC Issues
excerpt: A practical guide to diagnosing and fixing the most common PC problems — from blue screens to no internet.
content:
Every IT professional encounters PC issues regularly. Knowing how to systematically diagnose and fix problems saves time and keeps systems running. Here's a practical guide to the most common issues.

1. Computer Won't Turn On

Symptoms: No lights, no fan noise, completely dead.

  • Check the power cable and outlet
  • Test with a different power cable
  • Check the PSU switch on the back
  • Try a different outlet
  • If PSU is dead, replace it

2. Blue Screen of Death (BSOD)

Symptoms: System crashes with blue error screen.

  • Note the error code (e.g., 0x0000007B)
  • Boot into Safe Mode
  • Run Windows Memory Diagnostic
  • Update or rollback drivers
  • Check for Windows updates

3. Slow Performance

Symptoms: System takes forever to open apps or respond.

  • Check Task Manager for high CPU/memory usage
  • Disable unnecessary startup programs
  • Run disk cleanup and defragmentation
  • Check for malware with antivirus scan
  • Consider upgrading to SSD if using HDD

4. No Internet Connection

Symptoms: Browser can't load pages, "No internet" icon.

ipconfig /release     # Release IP
ipconfig /renew       # Get new IP
ipconfig /flushdns    # Clear DNS cache
netsh winsock reset   # Reset network stack

5. Printer Not Working

Symptoms: Print jobs stuck, printer offline, no response.

  • Check physical connections (USB, power)
  • Restart the print spooler service
  • Clear stuck print jobs
  • Update or reinstall printer drivers

These troubleshooting steps form the foundation of IT support. As you gain experience, you'll develop a systematic approach that helps you solve problems faster and more reliably.

title: CCTV Installation: A Beginner's Guide
excerpt: A practical guide to planning and installing a basic CCTV system for offices, schools, or homes.
content:
CCTV (Closed-Circuit Television) systems are essential for security in educational institutions, offices, and homes. Here's a practical guide to planning and installing a basic CCTV system.

1. Planning

Before buying any equipment, assess your needs:

  • Identify areas that need surveillance (entrances, corridors, labs)
  • Determine the number of cameras needed
  • Choose between wired and wireless systems
  • Decide on recording: NVR (Network Video Recorder) vs DVR
  • Plan cable routing and power supply locations

2. Equipment Needed

  • IP or analog cameras (depending on system)
  • NVR/DVR unit with storage
  • Cat6 Ethernet cables (for IP cameras)
  • Power supply units or PoE switches
  • Monitor for live viewing
  • Mounting brackets and screws

3. Installation Steps

  1. Mount cameras — Position at entry points and high-traffic areas, ensure good coverage
  2. Run cables — Route Ethernet or coaxial cables from cameras to NVR/DVR location
  3. Connect to NVR/DVR — Plug in all camera cables and power supply
  4. Configure the system — Set up recording schedules, motion detection, and alerts
  5. Test each camera — Verify live feed, recording, and playback on all channels

4. Maintenance Tips

  • Clean camera lenses regularly
  • Check cable connections and weatherproofing
  • Update firmware on NVR/DVR and cameras
  • Monitor storage capacity and manage old recordings
  • Test the system monthly

Proper CCTV installation provides peace of mind and deters unauthorized access. With practice, you can design systems that provide comprehensive coverage for any institution.
